summary: This memo gives an IAB recommendation for CIDR as a short-term strategy to stretch the life of the 32-bit IP address space and slow the growth of routing tables. It is historic.

eli5.summary: The Internet was running out of addresses and its routing tables were growing fast. This paper recommended a quick fix to buy time. It is historic.

subtitle: An emergency plan to extend the life of IPv4 addresses

tldr.problem: By the early 1990s, the Internet was growing exponentially. The 32-bit IPv4 address space was being consumed rapidly, and routing tables in core routers were growing so large they threatened to become unmanageable.
tldr.mechanism: CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) reorganizes IP address allocation and routing to be more efficient. Instead of assigning addresses in fixed-size blocks, it allows flexible block sizes. Routers aggregate address ranges, so one routing table entry can cover thousands of individual addresses.
tldr.outcome: CIDR successfully extended the life of IPv4 by a decade, but it was always intended as a temporary measure. The long-term solution is IPv6, which offers a vastly larger address space. The IAB endorsed CIDR and it became foundational to how the modern Internet assigns and routes addresses.

today: RFC 1481 is Historic. CIDR successfully extended the life of IPv4 and remains the basis for modern IP address allocation and routing. However, as the RFC anticipated, IPv4 addresses have become scarce, and IPv6 is gradually replacing IPv4 as the backbone protocol. This RFC is retained as a historical record of how the Internet addressed one of its greatest scaling challenges.

sections.title: The Scaling Crisis
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, the Internet experienced explosive growth. Two problems threatened to break the system. First, the supply of IPv4 addresses—32-bit numbers that uniquely identify computers—was being depleted rapidly. Each computer needed a unique address, and the space of 2^32 possible addresses seemed infinite until demand suddenly grew exponentially.

Second, core routers maintained routing tables that listed how to reach every network reachable from their location. As millions of new networks connected to the Internet, these tables grew from thousands of entries to hundreds of thousands. Storing and searching these giant tables became a bottleneck that threatened network performance.
sections.eli5: The Internet needed billions of unique addresses for all the computers connecting to it, but there were only enough for millions. And every router needed to remember how to reach every network, which was becoming impossible.

sections.title: CIDR: The Intermediate Solution
sections.content:
CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) is a set of practices for assigning and routing IP addresses more efficiently. It has two main parts.

First, address allocation became classless: instead of assigning addresses in fixed-size classes (where a block was either 16 million addresses or 65,536 or 256), the Internet Address Registry could assign a block of any convenient size. This reduced wasted addresses and accommodated networks of any size without waste.

Second, routing tables practice aggregation: if one organization controls a contiguous block of addresses, routers no longer list each subnetwork separately. Instead, they list the entire block with a single entry. This dramatically shrinks routing tables. The IAB endorsed CIDR in 1993, and it was rapidly deployed by router vendors, Internet service providers, and address registries.
sections.eli5: CIDR gives out addresses in exactly the sizes needed, and routers remember them in groups instead of individually. One entry covers a thousand addresses instead of listing them all.

sections.title: A Temporary Measure
sections.content:
The memo makes clear that CIDR was always intended as a short- to intermediate-term solution. It extends the life of the 32-bit IPv4 address space but does not solve the fundamental problem: IPv4 addresses are finite and the Internet's growth is exponential.

The long-term solution, endorsed by the Internet community, is IPv6, which uses 128-bit addresses and provides 2^96 times more addresses than IPv4. However, IPv6 is far more complex to deploy. CIDR served its purpose: it bought time for the Internet to grow from millions to billions of users while IPv6 was developed and gradually deployed.
sections.eli5: CIDR was meant to be a temporary fix while a bigger solution was being built. That bigger solution is IPv6, which has vastly more addresses.
